comments.author: @curiousunknown18
comments.text: The Bermuda Triangle sold 20 million books, scared an entire generation half to death, and turned out to be basically just a busy highway in bad weather — that's the greatest marketing con in the history of the ocean. Controversial take: Larry Kusche, the librarian who debunked the whole thing by just... reading the original records, is the most disrespectful person in this story, my man walked into a library and dismantled 70 years of mystery before lunch. But the part that genuinely got me is Bermuda fireworms rising exactly 56 hours after every full moon like clockwork — Columbus saw those little lights in 1492 and had no idea, and they were still doing the same show five centuries later. Thanks for sharing this one!

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That fireworm detail is genuinely one of the best "science is stranger than myth" facts out there - a bioluminescent display running like clockwork for 500+ years, hiding in plain sight the whole time anyone was busy inventing sea monsters. And fair point on Kusche - sometimes the most unglamorous work (actually reading the source records) is the most devastating.

comments.author: @giannisolga5191
comments.text: I remember that the Fastnet Race in 1979 in the Scilly Isles was witness to a storm of unsuspected magnitude, costing many of the world's best sailors their lives. As you say, where there is no scientific understanding of extreme natural events, myths arise. The human brain hates a vacuum. It will fill it with a myth, and that provides comfort and a sense of control.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That's a great real-world parallel - the 1979 Fastnet disaster is exactly the kind of extreme, poorly-understood-at-the-time event that could easily have spawned its own mythology if it had happened in a less charted stretch of ocean. Appreciate the connection.
